en.title: Linguistics: the whole course
en.short: What linguistics covers, how degrees are organised, the main areas and how to study them.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Linguistics is the systematic study of language: its sounds, words, sentences, meanings and use, and how people learn and store it. It is descriptive, not prescriptive. A linguist asks how a language works, not whether a speaker is being 'correct'.

It is not the same as learning many languages. Some linguists speak several; many do not. What they share is a method: collect examples of language, describe the pattern, and test the description against more data.

Linguistics matters outside the classroom. It informs reading and writing teaching, dictionary making, speech therapy, language policy, translation and the analysis of disputed texts.

sections.heading: How the degree is usually organised
sections.text:
Length, title and structure differ by country and institution, so check your own student handbook and department website before you plan.

In Nigeria a BA or BSc in Linguistics commonly runs four years, and many programmes combine Linguistics with a Nigerian language such as Yoruba, Igbo or Hausa. University programmes are accredited by the National Universities Commission (NUC). In the United Kingdom a first degree is usually three years; in the United States a bachelor’s degree is usually four; in South Africa a three-year BA is often followed by a one-year honours year. Master’s degrees usually take one to two years.

Most degrees move from compulsory foundations in the early years to optional specialist modules later, ending with a supervised project or dissertation.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order: the foundations
sections.text:
The introduction stage builds the core. It starts with what linguistics is and why language matters for society and for the mind. Then come the traditional levels, in the order most courses follow: phonetics (how speech sounds are made), the International Phonetic Alphabet and transcription, phonology (sound systems and patterns), morphology (word structure), syntax (phrases and sentences), semantics (meaning in words and sentences) and pragmatics (meaning in context).

An early module on language families places the languages of Africa in context. Niger-Congo is among the largest families in the world by number of languages, and Bantu is a branch of it. Afro-Asiatic includes Hausa, Arabic, Amharic and Somali. 'Khoisan' is often listed as a family, but many linguists now treat it as several unrelated families. Counts of languages vary with how languages and dialects are distinguished.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order: core and advanced work
sections.text:
The core stage applies the foundations. The history of English and historical and comparative linguistics show how languages change and how relationships between them are established. Language contact, pidgins and creoles explain what happens when speech communities meet. Sociolinguistics covers variation by region, class and situation; language policy covers decisions about which languages schools and governments use. Discourse analysis studies language beyond the sentence.

Further core modules connect linguistics to other work: psycholinguistics, first and second language acquisition and bilingualism, language teaching, lexicography and corpus linguistics, stylistics, writing systems, research methods and statistics for language data. The course ends with a project.

At master’s level the work is more advanced and more specialised: advanced phonology, advanced syntax, language documentation and endangered languages, and forensic linguistics.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Work with data, not only definitions. Transcribe a minute of your own speech, then a minute of a classmate’s. Take one sentence and divide it into words, morphemes, syllables and sounds.

Learn the IPA in small sets and use it. Reading symbols is passive; writing them from sound is the skill that is examined.

For theory, learn the argument and the evidence, not just the label. Keep a notebook of examples from every language you hear, and check each other’s transcriptions and tree diagrams in a study group.

sections.heading: Common mistakes students make
sections.text:
The commonest error is confusing letters with sounds. English spelling is a poor guide: 'ough' has several pronunciations, and one sound can be spelled many ways. Write sounds in square brackets, in IPA, and keep spelling separate.

Students also blur phonetics and phonology, or morphology and syntax. Many arrive believing linguistics means correcting grammar; it does not. Another fault is forcing English categories onto other languages, such as assuming every language marks tense.

In the project, small samples, unstated definitions and correlation presented as cause are frequent faults. In forensic work, do not claim more certainty than the method supports.

keyPoints: Linguistics describes how language works; it does not prescribe how people should speak.
Degree length, title and structure differ by country and institution, so check your own handbook.
The course follows the levels of language: sounds, sound systems, words, sentences, meaning and use.
Work with real language data, and learn the IPA by writing it, not only by reading it.
Keep spelling and sound apart, and do not force English categories onto other languages.
In research and in forensic work, claim only what your data and method can support.

en.title: What Is Linguistics?
en.short: Linguistics as the scientific study of language, its goals, branches, and key distinctions.

sections.heading: A science of language
sections.text:
Linguistics is the scientific study of language. It does not mean learning many languages. It means studying how language works: how sounds, words, sentences and meanings are organised, how people use language, and how it changes.

Like other sciences, linguistics observes evidence, forms hypotheses and tests them against data from speakers. Its goals are to describe languages accurately, explain the patterns found, and understand language as a human capacity. The evidence is usually spoken or written language, not the linguist’s opinion.

sections.heading: Describing, not correcting
sections.text:
A descriptive grammar records how a language is actually used by its speakers. A prescriptive grammar says how people should use it, often based on a standard variety or on rules borrowed from another language.

For example, a descriptive account may note that many English speakers say 'who did you see?' while a prescriptive rule may insist on 'whom'. The linguist does not deny that standard forms matter in exams or formal writing. The point is that description and prescription answer different questions.

sections.heading: Langue and parole
sections.text:
Ferdinand de Saussure, a founder of modern linguistics, distinguished langue from parole. Langue is the shared system of a language, the rules and contrasts that speakers carry in common. Parole is actual language use in particular situations.

A speaker may make a slip in parole, but the underlying langue remains systematic. This distinction helps linguists separate the stable system from individual acts of speech.

sections.heading: Branches and value
sections.text:
Linguistics has core branches: phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics. It also has other branches such as historical linguistics, and interdisciplinary fields such as sociolinguistics and psycholinguistics.

Every language is a complete system worth studying. All known languages have regular sound patterns, word structure, sentence structure and meaning. No language is primitive, and none is too simple for analysis. Judgements that one language is better often reflect social attitudes, not linguistic facts.

keyPoints: Linguistics is the scientific study of language, not the ability to speak many languages.
Descriptive grammar records actual usage; prescriptive grammar states rules for correct usage.
Saussure’s langue is the shared language system; parole is actual speech.
Core branches include phonetics, phonology, morphology, syntax, semantics and pragmatics.
Every language is a complete, systematic system; no language is primitive.
Linguists use evidence from speakers to describe and explain language.

en.title: Language in Society and the Human Mind
en.short: Design features, animal communication, language and thought, and the nature versus nurture debate.

sections.heading: Design features
sections.text: Human language has design features, properties that make it special. Charles Hockett listed several. Arbitrariness means the sound of a word does not naturally resemble its meaning. Duality of patterning means meaningless sounds combine into meaningful units, and units into sentences. Productivity, or open-endedness, lets speakers create and understand new sentences. Displacement lets people talk about past, future, absent or imaginary things. Cultural transmission means a child learns the language of the community rather than inheriting a fixed set of calls. Reflexiveness means language can describe itself.

sections.heading: Animals compared
sections.text: Animal communication is rich. Vervet monkeys in East Africa give different alarm calls for eagles, leopards and snakes, and other monkeys respond differently. This shows reference, but the calls are a small fixed set. No animal system studied has the full human set of design features. Some show displacement, as when honeybees dance to show the direction and distance of food. The difference is therefore one of degree and combination, not a simple line between speech and silence.

sections.heading: Language and thought
sections.text: Language, thought and culture affect one another. The Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, or linguistic relativity, asks whether the language we speak shapes how we think. The strong version, that language determines thought, is not supported. The weak version, that language influences some habits of attention and memory, has support in limited domains. Culture shapes vocabulary and ways of speaking, while language also helps transmit culture. For example, terms for kinship or colour differ across languages, but speakers can still learn new distinctions.

sections.heading: Nature and nurture
sections.text: The nature versus nurture debate asks how much language comes from biology and how much from experience. Nativists such as Noam Chomsky argue that children are born with a language faculty, sometimes called universal grammar. Behaviourists such as B. F. Skinner stressed imitation and reinforcement. Most linguists accept an interaction: children are biologically ready to learn language, but they need rich social input. Children produce rules they were not taught, such as 'goed' for 'went'.

keyPoints: Design features are properties such as arbitrariness, duality of patterning, productivity, displacement and cultural transmission.
Animal communication can be referential, but no studied system has the full set of human design features.
Linguistic relativity is the idea that language may influence thought; strong determinism is not supported.
Language and culture shape each other, and speakers can learn distinctions their language does not mark.
The nature versus nurture debate is best treated as an interaction between biological readiness and social input.
Children’s overregularisations such as 'goed' show rule learning, not simple imitation.

en.title: Articulatory Phonetics: How Speech Sounds Are Made
en.short: Speech organs, airstream, voicing, place and manner, and how consonants and vowels are described.

sections.heading: The speech organs
sections.text:
Speech starts with an airstream. Most English sounds use air pushed out from the lungs: a pulmonic egressive airstream. Air passes through the larynx, where the vocal folds sit, then through the pharynx and the mouth or nose.

Active articulators move: the lower lip, tongue tip, tongue blade and tongue body. Passive articulators include the upper lip, teeth, alveolar ridge, hard palate and soft palate. Lowering the soft palate lets air resonate in the nose.

sections.heading: Voicing and articulation
sections.text:
Voicing depends on the vocal folds. When they vibrate, a sound is voiced; when they are apart and do not vibrate, it is voiceless. The first sounds of “zip” and “sip” share place but differ in voicing.

Articulation has place and manner. Place is where the airstream is narrowed or stopped. Manner is how it is narrowed or stopped: complete closure gives a plosive, close narrowing gives a fricative, and a slow release after closure gives an affricate. Nasal, approximant and lateral are other manners.

sections.heading: Consonant descriptions
sections.text:
A consonant description usually gives voicing, place and manner, in that order. In English, the first sound of “tie” is a voiceless alveolar plosive; the first sound of “die” is a voiced alveolar plosive. The final sound of “sing” is a voiced velar nasal.

Other labels name the articulators involved or the shape of the airflow. Bilabial means both lips; labiodental means lower lip and upper teeth; velar means tongue body and soft palate. Lateral means air flows round the sides of the tongue. These labels describe English sounds, but the same terms apply to many languages.

sections.heading: Vowel descriptions
sections.text: Vowels are made with a relatively open vocal tract, without a central closure. They are described by tongue height, tongue backness and lip rounding, and sometimes by length or tenseness. For example, the vowel in “seat” is higher than the vowel in “sat” in many English accents. Accents differ, so describe the sound you hear, not the spelling.

keyPoints: Most speech sounds use a pulmonic egressive airstream from the lungs.
Voicing is vibration of the vocal folds; voiced sounds vibrate, voiceless sounds do not.
Place of articulation is where the airstream is narrowed or stopped; manner is how.
A consonant description usually gives voicing, place and manner, as in voiceless alveolar plosive.
Vowels are described by tongue height, backness and lip rounding, with length or tenseness sometimes added.
Accents vary, so describe the sound heard rather than the spelling.

en.title: The International Phonetic Alphabet and Transcription
en.short: How to use IPA symbols for broad and narrow transcription, including tone, length and stress.

sections.heading: The IPA as a standard
sections.text: The International Phonetic Alphabet, usually called the IPA, is a set of symbols for speech sounds. It was developed by the International Phonetic Association in the late nineteenth century and is revised from time to time. Its aim is one symbol for one sound, so that a transcription can be read by speakers of any language. The full chart lists consonants by place and manner and vowels by tongue position. Because the IPA is not tied to English spelling, it can write the sounds of English, Yoruba, Hausa, Swahili or any other language.

sections.heading: Broad and narrow
sections.text: Broad transcription, also called phonemic transcription, is written between slashes, as in /pɪn/. It records only sounds that contrast in a language. Narrow transcription is written between square brackets, as in [pʰɪn]. It adds details such as aspiration, the puff of air after p in many English accents. The word pin is therefore /pɪn/ broadly and [pʰɪn] narrowly for those speakers. Diacritics are small marks added to a symbol to show such detail. A transcription is not a spelling reform; it records pronunciation, and it varies with accent.

sections.heading: Tone, length and stress
sections.text: Tone is pitch used to distinguish words. IPA tone letters can follow a syllable: ˥ high, ˧ mid, ˩ low. In Yoruba, bá, ba and bà carry high, mid and low tone; in IPA they may be written [ba˥], [ba˧] and [ba˩]. Length is shown by ː after the symbol, so /a/ and /aː/ are short and long vowels in languages that contrast them. Stress is shown by ˈ before the stressed syllable and ˌ for secondary stress. In British English the noun record is /ˈrekɔːd/ and the verb record is /rɪˈkɔːd/.

keyPoints: The IPA is an international symbol set for speech sounds, not a spelling system.
Broad transcription uses slashes and records phonemes; narrow transcription uses brackets and adds phonetic detail.
The IPA chart organises consonants by place and manner and vowels by tongue position.
Tone can be written with tone letters such as ˥ ˧ ˩ or with diacritics on vowels.
Length is marked with ː and stress with ˈ or ˌ before the syllable.
Always state the accent or language, because transcription varies.

en.title: Phonology: Sound Systems and Patterns
en.short: Phonemes, allophones, features, rules, syllables, stress and tone, with English and African examples.

sections.heading: Phonetics and phonology
sections.text:
Phonetics studies speech sounds as physical events: how they are produced and heard. Phonology studies how one language organises those sounds into a system.

A phoneme is the smallest sound unit that distinguishes words. English /p/ and /b/ are separate phonemes because pin and bin are different words; such a pair is a minimal pair. An allophone is a variant of one phoneme: /p/ is [pʰ] in pin and plain [p] in spin, and the difference never changes meaning.

sections.heading: Allophones and features
sections.text:
Allophones usually stand in complementary distribution: each variant appears in its own fixed environment. English /l/ is clear before a vowel (leaf) and dark at the end of a syllable (feel).

Distinctive features describe a phoneme as a bundle of binary properties marked + or −: [+voice], [+nasal], [+continuant]. English /b/ is [+voice, −nasal]; /m/ is [+voice, +nasal]. The system, set out by Chomsky and Halle (1968), lets one rule name a whole natural class of sounds.

sections.heading: Rules and syllables
sections.text:
A phonological rule states a change and the environment where it applies: A → B / C __ D, read "A becomes B between C and D". The English plural shows assimilation: voiceless sounds take [s] (cats), voiced sounds take [z] (dogs), and after sibilants a syllable is added (horses).

A syllable has a nucleus, usually a vowel, with an optional onset and coda. English allows heavy clusters: strengths, /strɛŋkθs/, is CCCVCCCC. Swahili prefers open syllables and allows a syllabic nasal, as in mtu, "person".

sections.heading: Stress and tone
sections.text:
Stress is the prominence of a syllable, made by loudness, length and pitch. English stress can distinguish words: the noun REcord and the verb reCORD. Unstressed vowels often reduce to schwa, as in photograph and photography. Swahili is usually described as having regular penultimate stress, as in karibu.

Tone uses pitch to distinguish words. Yoruba has high, mid and low tones, so forms written igba can mean "calabash", "time" or "two hundred" according to their tones. Many West African and Bantu languages are tonal; English is not.

keyPoints: Phonetics studies the physical sounds; phonology studies how a language organises them into a system.
A phoneme distinguishes words, tested by minimal pairs; allophones are its context-bound variants.
Distinctive features describe phonemes as bundles of binary properties such as [+voice] and [+nasal].
A phonological rule is written A → B / C __ D, naming the change and the environment where it applies.
A syllable is onset, nucleus and coda, and languages differ in the clusters they allow.
Stress is syllable prominence and tone is pitch; both can distinguish words, as in English REcord and reCORD.

en.title: Morphology: The Structure of Words
en.short: Morphemes, roots, affixes, stems, inflection, derivation, compounding and reduplication.

sections.heading: Morphemes and roots
sections.text:
A morpheme is the smallest unit of language that carries meaning or grammatical function. Unhelpful has three: un- (not), help (assist), -ful (full of). A morpheme that can stand alone is free (help); one that cannot is bound (un-, -s).

The root is a word’s core, carrying its main meaning and not divisible further. In reactor the root is act. Some roots are bound: English ceive (receive, perceive), or Arabic k-t-b, which gives kataba (he wrote), kitāb (book) and kātib (writer).

sections.heading: Affixes, stems and bases
sections.text:
An affix is a bound morpheme added to a base: a prefix before it (re-read), a suffix after it (read-er), an infix inside it, a circumfix around it. Swahili stacks prefixes: ninakupenda (I love you) is ni- I + -na- present + ku- you + penda love.

The base is any form an affix attaches to. The stem is the base for inflection: in teachers, teach is the root, teacher the stem, -s the inflection. Base is wider: in unhelpfulness, help is the base for -ful, helpful the base for -ness.

sections.heading: Inflection and derivation
sections.text:
Inflection changes grammatical form without making a new word: walk, walks, walked; book, books. English keeps little inflection, but Turkish is rich: ev (house), evler (houses), evlerim (my houses), evlerimde (in my houses).

Derivation makes a new word, often changing word class: teach → teacher, happy → unhappy. Its meaning is often unpredictable, so dictionaries list derived words; inflection is usually regular and applies to whole classes.

sections.heading: Compounding and other processes
sections.text:
Compounding joins roots into one word: blackboard, sunflower, toothbrush. The last element usually sets the word class, so a sunflower is a flower.

Reduplication repeats a word or part of it: Indonesian rumah (house) → rumah-rumah (houses); English so-so, zig-zag. Other processes include conversion (email, noun to verb), clipping (advertisement → ad), blending (breakfast + lunch → brunch), acronyms (AIDS), back-formation (edit from editor) and borrowing (karaoke).

keyPoints: A morpheme is the smallest meaningful unit; it may be free (help) or bound (un-).
The root carries the core meaning, the stem is the base for inflection, and base is the wider term for anything an affix attaches to.
Inflection changes grammatical form (walk, walks) while derivation creates a new word, often of a different class (teach, teacher).
Compounding joins roots into one word (blackboard), and the last element usually decides the word class.
Reduplication repeats a word or part of it, as in Indonesian rumah-rumah (houses).
Other word formation processes include conversion, clipping, blending, acronyms, back-formation and borrowing.

en.title: Syntax Foundations: Phrases and Sentence Structure
en.short: Constituency, phrase structure rules, grammatical relations, tree diagrams and word order typology.

sections.heading: Constituency
sections.text: Constituency is the grouping of words into units that behave as a single part of a sentence. A constituent can be replaced by a pronoun, moved as a unit, or coordinated with a similar phrase. In “The child saw the dog”, “the child” and “the dog” are noun phrases (NPs), and “saw the dog” is a verb phrase (VP). The word “the” is a determiner, not a phrase; it cannot stand in for the whole NP.

sections.heading: Phrase rules and trees
sections.text:
Phrase structure rules state which units may combine. For English: S -> NP VP; VP -> V NP; NP -> Det N. The arrow means “can be rewritten as”. A tree diagram shows the same information in levels. For the sentence above:

        S
      /   \
    NP     VP
   / \     / \
 Det  N   V   NP
  |   |   |  / \
 The child saw Det N
              |   |
             the dog

The subject NP is a daughter of S and a sister of VP. The object NP is inside VP and a sister of V. Trees make the hierarchy visible.

sections.heading: Grammatical relations
sections.text: Grammatical relations are the roles phrases play in the sentence. The subject is the NP that the verb agrees with in English: “The child sees” not “The child see”. The object is the NP that follows a transitive verb and completes its meaning: “the dog” in “saw the dog”. Subjects often control agreement; objects are often affected by the action. These are English patterns, not universal definitions.

sections.heading: Word order typology
sections.text: Word order typology compares how languages arrange subject (S), verb (V) and object (O). English is mainly SVO. Many languages are SOV, and some are VSO. VSO order occurs in a number of African languages, and SVO and SOV are also widespread on the continent. Order affects phrase structure: in a VSO language the verb may combine with the subject and object in a different hierarchy from English. When you draw trees for another language, use that language’s rules, not English ones.

keyPoints: Constituents are word groups that act as single units; substitution, movement and coordination help test them.
Phrase structure rules such as S -> NP VP and VP -> V NP describe possible combinations.
In an English tree the subject NP is sister to VP, and the object NP is sister to V inside VP.
Subject and object are grammatical relations; they are language-particular patterns, not universal definitions.
Word order typology compares S, V and O; English is mainly SVO, while SOV and VSO also occur, including in African languages.
Draw trees using the rules of the language being analysed, not English rules.

en.title: Semantics: Meaning in Words and Sentences
en.short: It covers sense and reference, word relations, componential analysis, sentence meaning, entailment and contradiction.

sections.heading: Sense and reference
sections.text: Semantics studies literal meaning in language. The sense of an expression is its place in the language: the meaning that relates it to other words. The reference is the thing or set of things in the world that it points to. 'The morning star' and 'the evening star' have different senses but the same reference, the planet Venus. A word may have sense without reference: 'unicorn' has a sense but no real referent.

sections.heading: Word relations
sections.text: Synonymy is sameness or close similarity of sense: 'begin' and 'start' are near synonyms; exact synonyms are rare. Antonymy is oppositeness: 'hot' and 'cold' are gradable, 'alive' and 'dead' are complementary, and 'buy' and 'sell' are relational. Hyponymy is inclusion: 'cow' is a hyponym of 'animal'; 'animal' is the hypernym. Polysemy is one word with several related senses: 'head' can mean a body part, the top of something, or a leader.

sections.heading: Componential analysis
sections.text: Componential analysis describes word meaning with semantic features, usually written plus or minus. Take four words: man [+human, +adult, +male], woman [+human, +adult, −male], boy [+human, −adult, +male], girl [+human, −adult, −male]. The features show what the words share and where they differ. The method works best for clear-cut sets such as kinship terms or animals; it struggles with abstract and context-dependent words.

sections.heading: Sentence meaning
sections.text: The meaning of a sentence depends on the meanings of its words and on syntax, the way they are combined. Semantics often states sentence meaning as truth conditions: the situations in which the sentence is true. Entailment is a relation between sentences. A entails B when, whenever A is true, B must also be true. 'Ada killed the goat' entails 'the goat died'. Contradiction is a sentence that cannot be true: 'This bachelor is married' is contradictory if bachelor means an unmarried man. Two sentences contradict each other when they cannot both be true.

keyPoints: Sense is an expression’s meaning inside the language; reference is what it points to in the world.
Synonymy is similarity of sense, antonymy is oppositeness, and hyponymy is inclusion under a broader term.
Polysemy is one word with several related senses, such as 'head' as body part, top, or leader.
Componential analysis represents meaning with features such as [+human] and [+male].
A sentence’s meaning depends on word meanings and syntax, and can be stated as its truth conditions.
A entails B when A cannot be true while B is false; a contradiction cannot be true.

en.title: Pragmatics: Meaning in Context
en.short: Sentence versus utterance meaning, deixis, speech acts, implicature, Grice’s maxims and politeness.

sections.heading: Sentence and utterance
sections.text: Semantics studies meaning in words and sentences; pragmatics studies what a speaker means in context. A sentence is an abstract string with a literal meaning. An utterance is a sentence used by someone, at a time and place, for a purpose. “It is cold in here” has the sentence meaning that the temperature is low. Said beside an open window, it may be an utterance meaning a request to close it. The same sentence can carry different meanings in different contexts.

sections.heading: Deixis and speech acts
sections.text: Deixis is meaning that depends on context: I and you (person), here and there (place), now and tomorrow (time). Without context, these words do not pick out a referent. Speech act theory says utterances do things. A direct speech act matches form to function: “Close the door” is an order. An indirect speech act uses one form for another function: “Could you close the door?” is a question in form but a request in function. Austin distinguished the locutionary act (what is said), the illocutionary act (what is done) and the perlocutionary act (its effect).

sections.heading: Implicature and cooperation
sections.text: Conversational implicature is an extra meaning that a hearer infers. H. P. Grice proposed the cooperative principle: speakers try to be informative, truthful, relevant and clear. Its maxims are quantity, quality, relation and manner. When a speaker openly breaks a maxim, the hearer looks for a reason. A: “Did all the students pass?” B: “Some passed.” The sentence meaning of some does not exclude all. The utterance implicates that not all passed, because a fully informative answer would have said all if true.

sections.heading: Politeness
sections.text: Brown and Levinson’s politeness theory explains why speakers mean less directly. Face is self-image. Positive face is the wish to be liked; negative face is the wish not to be imposed on. Positive politeness shows closeness: “We should close that window.” Negative politeness shows respect for freedom: “Could you possibly close the window?” It depends on distance, power and imposition.

keyPoints: Pragmatics studies speaker meaning in context, while semantics studies literal sentence meaning.
An utterance is a sentence used at a particular time and place, so context fixes deixis such as here, now and you.
Speech act theory shows that utterances perform actions; Austin separated locutionary, illocutionary and perlocutionary acts.
Grice’s cooperative principle and its maxims of quantity, quality, relation and manner explain conversational implicature.
Flouting a maxim invites the hearer to infer an extra meaning, as when “some passed” implicates “not all”.
Brown and Levinson’s politeness theory uses face, positive politeness and negative politeness to explain indirect wording.

en.title: Language Families and the Languages of Africa
en.short: Comparative method, genetic classification, African language phyla, Bantu expansion, areal features and contact.

sections.heading: Comparing languages
sections.text: The comparative method reconstructs earlier languages by comparing related languages. Linguists look for cognates, words with a shared origin, and for regular sound correspondences, not just similar meanings. If /p/ in one language regularly matches /f/ in another across many words, that pattern supports common descent. A language family is a group of languages descended from one ancestor, or proto-language. Genetic classification groups languages by that descent. It is not the same as mutual intelligibility or shared typology.

sections.heading: African language groups
sections.text: African languages are usually grouped into several phyla, meaning major families. Afroasiatic includes Arabic, Hausa, Amharic, Somali and Berber. Nilo-Saharan includes Luo, Kanuri and Dinka. Niger-Congo includes Yoruba, Igbo, Wolof, Fula and the Bantu languages. Khoisan is a convenient label for southern African click languages such as Khoekhoe and the San languages, but many scholars do not treat it as one genetic family. Malagasy, in Madagascar, is Austronesian, not African in origin. Classification boundaries are debated.

sections.heading: Niger-Congo and Bantu
sections.text: Niger-Congo is one of the world’s largest families by number of languages. Its Bantu branch covers much of central, eastern and southern Africa. Bantu speakers spread from a homeland in west-central Africa over several thousand years. The expansion is linked with farming and perhaps iron working, though causes are debated. Swahili, Zulu, Xhosa, Kikuyu and Lingala are Bantu languages. Bantu languages often share noun class systems and agreement prefixes; for example, Swahili wa- marks human plural in watu 'people' and wanafunzi 'students'.

sections.heading: Areal features and contact
sections.text: An areal feature is a trait shared by neighbouring languages because of contact, not inheritance. Clicks in Xhosa and Zulu, Bantu languages, were borrowed from Khoisan languages. West African languages across different families often share labial-velar stops such as /kp/. Contact also produces borrowing, multilingualism and lingua francas. Swahili serves as a lingua franca in East Africa, and Hausa in West Africa. Areal and genetic explanations must be kept apart.

keyPoints: The comparative method uses cognates and regular sound correspondences to reconstruct proto-languages.
A language family is a group descended from a common ancestor; genetic classification is not typology or mutual intelligibility.
Africa’s main groups include Afroasiatic, Nilo-Saharan and Niger-Congo; Khoisan is a debated label, and Malagasy is Austronesian.
Niger-Congo is one of the world’s largest families, and Bantu is its widespread branch.
Bantu expansion spread Bantu languages from west-central Africa over several thousand years; causes are debated.
Areal features such as clicks in Xhosa and Zulu come from contact, not inheritance.

en.title: The History of the English Language
en.short: Old English to Modern English: sound change, borrowing, standardisation and global spread.

sections.heading: Old English
sections.text:
English began as a West Germanic dialect brought to Britain from the fifth century by settlers from northern Europe, often called Angles, Saxons and Jutes.

Old English, the period up to about 1150, was heavily inflected: nouns, adjectives and pronouns changed form for case, number and gender. Its vocabulary was mostly Germanic, with early Latin and Celtic borrowings and later Norse influence. Beowulf is the best-known long poem.

sections.heading: Middle English
sections.text:
The Norman Conquest of 1066 made French the language of court and administration for a time. English continued among ordinary people.

By the Middle English period, roughly 1150 to 1500, endings had weakened and word order became more important. Thousands of words came from French and Latin, such as justice, parliament and study. Chaucer wrote in Middle English. Borrowing means taking a word from another language.

sections.heading: Early Modern English
sections.text:
Early Modern English, roughly 1500 to 1700, saw the Great Vowel Shift. This was a chain of sound changes in which long vowels were raised, and the two highest ones became diphthongs, a diphthong being two vowel sounds in one syllable.

For example, the vowel in house moved from a long 'oo' type sound towards the modern sound, while spelling stayed. Printing, introduced by William Caxton in the 1470s, helped fix spellings. Renaissance borrowing added many Latin and Greek words.

sections.heading: Standardisation and spread
sections.text:
Standard English grew through printing, schooling, dictionaries and official use, not in a single moment. Samuel Johnson’s Dictionary appeared in 1755.

From the seventeenth century, British trade, settlement and empire carried English to North America, the Caribbean, India, Australia and Africa. In Africa, countries such as Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa use English in education, government or business, often as a second language. Local varieties, including African Englishes, have their own vocabulary and pronunciation. Modern English is therefore a family of varieties, not one uniform speech.

keyPoints: Old English was a heavily inflected West Germanic language; Middle English lost many endings and borrowed heavily from French and Latin.
The Great Vowel Shift was a chain of long-vowel changes in Early Modern English that changed pronunciation but not spelling.
Borrowing is taking words from another language; English borrowed from Celtic, Norse, Latin, French, Greek and many others.
Standard English developed gradually through printing, schooling, dictionaries and official use, not by one decree.
British trade, settlement and empire spread English to North America, the Caribbean, India, Australia and Africa.
English in Africa is often a second language and exists in local varieties such as Nigerian or Kenyan English.

en.title: Historical and Comparative Linguistics
en.short: The comparative method, sound laws, proto-form reconstruction, and contact versus inheritance.

sections.heading: Cognates and correspondence
sections.text: Historical linguistics studies how languages change over time. Comparative linguistics compares related languages to reconstruct their ancestor. Cognates are words in different languages that descend from the same word in a common ancestor. The comparative method is the procedure of comparing cognates to find regular sound correspondences. A sound correspondence is a recurring pair of sounds in the same position in cognate words. It is regular when it appears in many words, not just one. For example, English ten, tooth and tongue have initial /t/, while German zehn, Zahn and Zunge have initial /ts/, written z. In these inherited words, English /t/ corresponds to German /ts/.

sections.heading: Sound laws and analogy
sections.text: The Neogrammarians, a late nineteenth-century German school, argued that sound change is regular and exceptionless. A sound law applies mechanically to every word with the same sound in the same environment. Apparent exceptions, they said, come from analogy, borrowing or dialect mixing. Analogy is change by which a form is remade on the pattern of other forms. For example, English plural cows replaced older kine by analogy with regular plurals such as stones. Modern linguists still treat regular sound change as the working assumption of the comparative method, while allowing some sporadic exceptions.

sections.heading: Reconstructing proto forms
sections.text: To reconstruct a proto form, list cognates, establish correspondences, assign a proto sound to each correspondence, and mark the result with an asterisk (*), meaning unattested. From English /t/ : German /ts/, we reconstruct initial *t for the ancestor of ten/zehn, tooth/Zahn and tongue/Zunge. A full proto form needs more evidence. Genetic relationship means descent from a common ancestor, shown by regular correspondences. Areal relationship means contact: languages share features through borrowing or a Sprachbund, a contact area. Borrowing copies words or patterns and can create lookalikes that are not cognates.

sections.heading: Divergence and contact
sections.text: Divergence is the splitting of one speech community into separate varieties that change apart. A family tree models divergence, but contact can spread features across branches. So linguists compare many words and check regular correspondences before claiming kinship.

keyPoints: The comparative method compares cognates to find regular sound correspondences.
Neogrammarians held that sound change is regular and exceptionless; analogy, borrowing and dialect mixing explain apparent exceptions.
Reconstructed proto forms are marked with an asterisk because they are unattested.
Genetic relationship rests on descent from a common ancestor, while areal relationship rests on contact.
Borrowing can create similar words that are not cognates, so check many regular correspondences.
Divergence and contact both shape language history, so family trees are models, not complete facts.

en.title: Language Contact, Pidgins and Creoles
en.short: Borrowing, code switching, diglossia, multilingual repertoires, and how pidgins and creoles form.

sections.heading: Contact and borrowing
sections.text: Language contact happens when speakers of different languages interact regularly. Borrowing is the taking of a word or pattern from one language into another, usually adapted to the borrower’s sounds and grammar. English has borrowed safari from Swahili and tsunami from Japanese. Borrowing differs from code switching because the borrowed item becomes part of the receiving language and is used by monolinguals too.

sections.heading: Switching and repertoires
sections.text: Code switching is the alternation between languages or varieties within a conversation. It may occur between sentences or inside one sentence, and it often carries social meaning, such as marking identity or emphasis. A multilingual repertoire is the set of languages and varieties a speaker can draw on, with the situations in which each is used. Repertoires are not equal boxes: a speaker may be strong in one language for home talk and another for school writing. Example: Ngozi speaks Igbo at home, Nigerian Pidgin in the market and English at university. Her switching follows social rules.

sections.heading: Diglossia
sections.text: Diglossia is a stable arrangement in which two varieties of one language, or two languages, serve different functions. A high variety is used in formal writing, religion or education, and a low variety in ordinary conversation. Charles Ferguson described this pattern, and Joshua Fishman extended the idea to separate languages in a community. Diglossia is not the same as bilingualism: a person may be bilingual without living in a diglossic society.

sections.heading: Pidgins and creoles
sections.text: A pidgin is a contact language that develops among speakers with no common language, for trade or labour. It is rule-governed, not broken speech. Its vocabulary comes mostly from a lexifier, the language that supplies most of its words, while its grammar shows substrate influence from the speakers’ local languages. A creole is a contact language that has become a community’s first language and expanded. English-based creoles include Krio in Sierra Leone and Jamaican Creole. Nigerian Pidgin is English-lexified and used as a lingua franca; many scholars describe it as an expanded pidgin, and some call it a creole because it has native speakers.

keyPoints: Borrowing takes words or patterns into a language and adapts them; code switching alternates languages within talk.
A multilingual repertoire is the set of languages and varieties a speaker uses across different situations.
Diglossia is a stable division of functions between a high and a low variety, not simply bilingualism.
A pidgin is a rule-governed contact language, not broken speech, with a lexifier and substrate influence.
A creole is a contact language that has become a community’s first language and expanded; not every creole has a recorded pidgin stage.
Nigerian Pidgin is English-lexified and used as a lingua franca; Krio and Jamaican Creole are English-based creoles.

en.title: Sociolinguistics: Variation and Social Meaning
en.short: Regional, class, gender, age and ethnic variation, methods, style shifting, networks and attitudes.

sections.heading: Variation and social factors
sections.text: Sociolinguists study how language varies with region and social position. Regional variation is mapped by dialectology: an isogloss is a line on a map marking where a feature stops. Social class is usually measured by occupation, education and income; higher-status speakers often use more standard variants in formal styles. Gender, age and ethnicity matter too, but they are not fixed causes. Gender variation reflects identities and norms, not biology. Age can show age grading, where a feature marks a life stage, or generational change. Ethnicity can involve dialect features or language choice. In African cities, Nigerian Pidgin, Sheng and Tsotsitaal show these factors interacting.

sections.heading: Methods and sampling
sections.text: Variationist methods collect comparable speech from a sample. A sociolinguistic interview combines casual talk, a reading passage and a word list to elicit styles from casual to careful. Rapid anonymous surveys record a feature without a full interview. Matched-guise tests play the same speaker in different accents to measure attitudes. Recordings are coded for variants and analysed with statistics, often multivariate models.

sections.heading: Style, communities, networks
sections.text: Style shifting is a speaker’s adjustment of formality or dialect to addressee, setting and topic. Labov linked it to attention to speech; Bell’s audience design says speakers respond to their audience. A speech community is a group sharing norms for using and interpreting language. Social networks matter: dense, multiplex networks, where people know each other in several roles, tend to enforce local vernacular norms; loose networks favour standard or new forms. In a Lagos market, a trader named Ada may use Yoruba with an older customer, Nigerian Pidgin with a peer, and English with a bank official. The shift signals identity and situation.

sections.heading: Attitudes and urban Africa
sections.text: Language attitudes are evaluations of varieties and speakers. They can be positive or negative and may be unconscious. In urban Africa, variation often tracks education, ethnicity, age and mobility. A Nairobi student may use Sheng with friends and English in a seminar. Variation carries social meaning, not disorder. Researchers must obtain consent and respect speakers.

keyPoints: Sociolinguistic variation is systematic and carries social meaning.
Regional variation is mapped with isoglosses; social class, gender, age and ethnicity interact.
Variationist methods sample comparable speech through interviews, reading passages, word lists and rapid surveys; matched-guise tests measure attitudes.
Style shifting adjusts formality or dialect to addressee, setting and topic.
A speech community shares norms for language use; dense multiplex networks tend to enforce vernacular norms.
Language attitudes are evaluations of varieties and speakers and can be measured with matched-guise tests.

en.title: Language Policy, Planning and Education
en.short: Status, corpus and acquisition planning, policy bodies, African comparisons and the medium of instruction.

sections.heading: Three kinds of planning
sections.text:
Language policy sets which languages are used, taught and developed; language planning carries it out. Status planning decides a language’s functions, such as official, court, school or media use. Corpus planning develops the language through spelling, dictionaries, terminology and standard forms.

Acquisition planning covers who learns what, when and how, including teacher training, textbooks and literacy. Prestige planning, which raises a language’s public image, is sometimes added. The types overlap: official status usually needs corpus work and teaching.

sections.heading: Who makes policy
sections.text:
Governments, parliaments and ministries of education make national policy. Specialist bodies advise or do corpus work.

In Nigeria the Federal Ministry of Education issues the National Policy on Education, and the Nigerian Educational Research and Development Council (NERDC) prepares curriculum and materials. South Africa’s Pan South African Language Board (PanSALB) promotes official languages. Tanzania’s National Kiswahili Council (Baraza la Kiswahili la Taifa) develops Kiswahili. The African Union’s African Academy of Languages (ACALAN) supports African languages. UNESCO advises but does not make national law.

sections.heading: African comparisons
sections.text:
Tanzania uses Kiswahili as the main primary medium and English in secondary schools. South Africa’s Constitution recognises many official languages, and its 1997 Language in Education Policy supports mother-tongue based bilingual education, though practice varies.

Kenya’s policy encourages the language of the catchment area in early primary and English later. Nigeria’s National Policy on Education favours the mother tongue or language of the immediate community in early primary, with English later. Implementation is uneven because of teacher supply, exams, parents’ preferences and publishing.

sections.heading: Medium of instruction
sections.text:
The medium of instruction (MOI) is the language used to teach subjects. A strong first-language base can help literacy, while an early switch to a second language may slow understanding if teachers and books are unprepared.

Policy must match exams, teacher training and materials. In a Kano primary class, a teacher may begin in Hausa and move to English, but if textbooks are only in English the plan fails. The choice is educational and political.

keyPoints: Status planning allocates functions; corpus planning develops the language; acquisition planning organises learning.
National policy is made by governments and ministries, with specialist councils advising and doing corpus work.
Nigeria’s National Policy on Education favours early mother tongue or community language, with English later.
Tanzania, South Africa, Kenya and Nigeria share mother-tongue provisions but implementation varies.
The medium of instruction affects learning, and it must match teacher training, exams and materials.
Language policy is both educational and political, so evidence and local views matter.

en.title: Discourse Analysis and Conversation
en.short: This summary covers cohesion, coherence, information structure, turn taking and worked analysis of texts and talk.

sections.heading: Text and cohesion
sections.text: Discourse analysis studies language in stretches longer than a sentence: paragraphs, conversations, speeches and messages. Cohesion is the visible linking of text through grammar and vocabulary. Halliday and Hasan describe reference (pronouns such as she or it), substitution (one, do so), ellipsis (leaving words out), conjunction (but, therefore) and lexical cohesion (repetition, synonyms, word groups). Cohesion helps a reader follow, but it does not guarantee sense.

sections.heading: Coherence and topic
sections.text: Coherence is the underlying sense of unity: the ideas connect logically and fit the context and the reader’s knowledge. A text can be cohesive yet incoherent. Topic is what a sentence is about; the comment says something about it. Information structure concerns given and new information. Writers usually put given information early and new, important information late, where it receives end-focus. Theme is the starting point of a clause; rheme is the rest. In “The committee met on Monday. It postponed the vote”, it refers back to the committee, so the link is cohesive and coherent.

sections.heading: Turns and sequence
sections.text: Conversation analysis studies how talk is organised turn by turn. Speakers orient to transition relevance places, points where a turn may end. Turn taking is managed through current-speaker selects next, next-speaker self-selects, or current speaker continues. Adjacency pairs are paired turns such as question and answer or greeting and greeting. Preference organisation means some responses are expected; a dispreferred response, such as a refusal, is usually delayed and softened. Repair is the fixing of trouble in hearing or understanding. Backchannels such as “mm” show attention without claiming a full turn.

sections.heading: Worked dialogue
sections.text: A: Have you paid the rent? B: I went to the bank, but the queue was long. B’s answer is coherent only by inference: the long queue is offered as a reason for not paying. The question and answer form an adjacency pair; the reply is a dispreferred response. “But” is a cohesive conjunction, and the reply ends with the reason, “the queue was long”, which carries end-focus.

keyPoints: Cohesion is surface linking through reference, substitution, ellipsis, conjunction and lexical ties.
Coherence is the underlying logical and contextual unity that makes a text make sense.
Information structure organises given and new information, often placing new focus late.
Conversation analysis examines turn taking, transition relevance places, adjacency pairs, preference and repair.
A dispreferred response such as a refusal is typically delayed and softened.
In the worked dialogue, the answer is coherent by inference and forms the second part of an adjacency pair.

en.title: Psycholinguistics: Language in the Mind
en.short: Speech perception, lexical access, sentence processing, production models, reading, slips and aphasia.

sections.heading: Speech and words
sections.text:
Speech perception turns a continuous sound stream into discrete units. Categorical perception means that sounds varying along a physical continuum are heard as a few discrete phoneme categories, not as a gradual blend. The McGurk effect shows vision’s role: seeing one mouth shape while hearing another can change what is heard. Phoneme restoration fills a missing sound from context.

The mental lexicon stores word forms, meanings and links. Lexical access matches input to that store and is affected by frequency and context. In priming, one word speeds recognition of a related word, supporting a network view.

sections.heading: Sentence processing
sections.text: Sentence processing builds structure and meaning in real time. In a garden-path sentence such as “The horse raced past the barn fell”, readers first take raced as the main verb, then reanalyse. Syntax-first models claim structure is built before meaning is fully used. Constraint-based models claim syntax, meaning, frequency and context compete from the start. Working memory limits the structure held active.

sections.heading: Producing language
sections.text: Levelt’s production model has stages: conceptualising the message, formulating words and syntax, articulating sounds, and monitoring output. Slips of the tongue, such as “tip of the slung” for “slip of the tongue”, exchange sounds within planning units. They suggest that speech is planned in chunks and that speakers monitor and repair it.

sections.heading: Reading and aphasia
sections.text:
Reading uses the lexicon and sentence system plus visual recognition. The dual-route model proposes a lexical route for known words and a sublexical route that converts letters to sounds. Eye movements show reading proceeds in fixations and jumps.

Aphasia is acquired language impairment after brain damage. Broca’s aphasia often makes speech nonfluent and effortful; Wernicke’s aphasia often affects comprehension, but individual patterns vary. Double dissociations, where different patients lose different language abilities, support separable language components in the brain, though no single area controls all language.

keyPoints: Speech perception is categorical and multimodal; the McGurk effect shows vision can alter what is heard.
The mental lexicon stores word forms and meanings; lexical access is faster for frequent and primed words.
Garden-path sentences show reanalysis; syntax-first and constraint-based models disagree about when meaning is used.
Levelt’s model stages production from message to articulation, with monitoring.
Slips of the tongue exchange sounds within planning units, revealing chunked planning.
Broca’s and Wernicke’s aphasia often affect production and comprehension respectively, but patterns vary and double dissociations support separable components.

en.title: First Language Acquisition: From Babbling to Grammar
en.short: Babbling to multiword speech, acquisition theories, critical period, sound, grammar and meaning.

sections.heading: From babble to sentences
sections.text: Prelinguistic stages move from cooing to babbling, repeated syllables such as “bababa”, typically from about six months. Canonical babbling uses adult-like syllables. First words appear around the first birthday, often as holophrases: one word carries a whole message, as when “milk” means “I want milk”. Around eighteen to twenty-four months, children produce two-word telegraphic speech, omitting grammatical words: “Mummy shoe”. Multiword speech follows. Ages vary; these are typical landmarks, not fixed rules.

sections.heading: Nativist and interactionist
sections.text: Behaviourism, linked to B.F. Skinner, explained acquisition by imitation and reinforcement, but novel errors such as “goed” weakened it. Nativism, associated with Noam Chomsky, argues that children are born with a language faculty, often called universal grammar, which guides acquisition from limited input. Interactionists stress that adults and peers scaffold the child: child-directed speech, joint attention and turn-taking make language learnable. Meaning is negotiated in routines such as feeding and play. Both views agree input matters; they disagree on how much structure is innate.

sections.heading: Usage-based and critical period
sections.text: Usage-based theories, linked to Michael Tomasello, reject a separate grammar module. Children build constructions, or form-meaning patterns, from frequent utterances, intention-reading and analogy. Hearing “more juice” and “more tickles”, a child generalises “more X”. The critical period debate asks whether acquisition must happen within a sensitive window. Lenneberg linked it to brain maturation. Evidence from late signers and isolated children is suggestive but difficult. Most researchers accept a sensitive period for phonology and grammar, not a strict cut-off.

sections.heading: Sound, grammar, meaning
sections.text: Sound acquisition starts before words. Infants discriminate many speech contrasts, then perceptual narrowing tunes them to the ambient language by the end of the first year. Vowel and consonant accuracy improves gradually. Grammar grows from holophrases to combinations and morphology; overregularisation, as in “mouses”, shows a working rule, not imitation. Meaning begins with fast mapping, guessing a new word’s sense after one exposure. Children may overextend words, calling all animals “dog”, or underextend them.

keyPoints: Children typically move from cooing and babbling to first words, two-word telegraphic speech and then multiword speech; ages vary.
Nativism holds that an innate language faculty or universal grammar guides acquisition.
Interactionists emphasise child-directed speech, joint attention and scaffolding in social routines.
Usage-based accounts explain grammar as constructions learned from frequent utterances and intention-reading.
The critical period debate concerns a sensitive window, especially for phonology and grammar; evidence is suggestive, not a strict cut-off.
Sound perception narrows to the ambient language, grammar shows rule-based errors such as “goed”, and meaning grows through fast mapping and overextension.

en.title: Second Language Acquisition and Bilingualism
en.short: Interlanguage, error analysis, transfer, fossilisation, input, interaction, motivation and contrastive analysis.

sections.heading: Interlanguage and transfer
sections.text:
Interlanguage is the learner’s own rule system, between the first language and the target language. Selinker (1972) described it as systematic and changing. Error analysis studies errors to reveal those rules and separates an error, a systematic wrong rule, from a mistake, a slip the learner can correct. Transfer is first-language influence: positive when rules match, negative when they differ. The contrastive analysis hypothesis, linked to Lado (1957), predicted difficulty from differences, but its strong form failed because many errors are developmental and shared across first languages.

A Yoruba-speaking pupil in Nigeria may write “I saw boy” for “I saw the boy”, because Yoruba has no word for “the”. Error analysis of real work is needed; transfer explains only some errors.

sections.heading: Input and interaction
sections.text:
Fossilisation is the stabilisation of a wrong feature in the interlanguage despite exposure and instruction. Input is the language the learner hears or reads. Krashen’s input hypothesis says acquisition needs comprehensible input slightly beyond the current level, often written i + 1, but input alone is not enough. The interaction hypothesis, linked to Long, stresses negotiation of meaning: learners ask for clarification, repeat and reformulate, and so notice gaps. Feedback and modified output support this.

In large classes, pair work and information-gap tasks increase interaction. Clear English, visuals and controlled texts help before freer use.

sections.heading: Motivation and bilingualism
sections.text:
Motivation is the drive to learn. Gardner and Lambert distinguished integrative motivation, a wish to connect with the target-language community, from instrumental motivation, a practical goal such as an exam or a job. Intrinsic motivation comes from interest; extrinsic motivation comes from rewards or pressure. Strong motivation supports persistence, and success builds motivation.

Bilingualism is the use of two or more languages. Additive bilingualism adds a second language while maintaining the first; subtractive bilingualism replaces it. In many African classrooms, respecting learners’ languages can support confidence. English teaching should combine meaningful input, interaction, focused error feedback and realistic goals.

keyPoints: Interlanguage is a systematic, changing learner rule system between the first and target languages.
Error analysis distinguishes systematic errors from slips and treats errors as evidence of learning.
Transfer can be positive or negative, but the strong contrastive analysis hypothesis failed because many errors are developmental.
Fossilisation is a stabilised wrong feature that persists despite input and instruction.
Comprehensible input is necessary but not sufficient; interaction and modified output help learners notice gaps.
Motivation and additive bilingualism support persistence, so English teaching should combine meaning, interaction, feedback and realistic goals.

en.title: Linguistics and Language Teaching
en.short: How linguistic analysis informs reading, writing, grammar, pronunciation, literacy and error correction.

sections.heading: Analysis into teaching
sections.text: Applied linguistics uses descriptions of language to make teaching decisions. A descriptive grammar records what speakers do; a pedagogical grammar selects and orders what learners need. Analysis of the target language, the learners’ first language and the classroom task helps a teacher choose examples, sequence and focus. It does not dictate one method. The teacher still judges what is useful for a particular group.

sections.heading: Reading and writing
sections.text: Reading needs decoding and comprehension. Phonics teaching links letters to sounds; phonological awareness is the ability to notice and manipulate sounds. In a second language, learners may transfer first-language literacy, but oral proficiency and orthography also matter. Writing needs control of spelling and grammar plus genre, cohesion and audience. Analysis of texts shows the moves and linking words a genre uses. A teacher can make these visible.

sections.heading: Grammar and pronunciation
sections.text: Grammar teaching can be explicit, with rules and terms, or implicit, through examples and use. Corpus analysis shows frequent patterns, so a syllabus can teach common forms first. Pronunciation teaching aims at intelligibility, not a native accent. It uses phoneme contrasts, stress and intonation. Minimal pairs, such as ship and sheep, train listening and production. Teachers should check which contrasts matter in the learners’ setting.

sections.heading: Errors and awareness
sections.text: An error shows a learner’s developing system, called interlanguage; a mistake is a slip the learner can self-correct. Error analysis looks at patterns, not single faults. Corrective feedback can be direct or indirect, immediate or delayed. Too much correction can stop fluency. Focus on form means briefly drawing attention to a language point during meaningful work. Language awareness makes learners notice how language works. In a case, Mrs Adeyemi’s class sorts walked, played and wanted by the ending’s sound: /t/, /d/ and /ɪd/. This links grammar, spelling and pronunciation.

keyPoints: Applied linguistics uses language description to inform teaching choices, not to impose one method.
Reading requires decoding and comprehension; writing requires genre, cohesion and audience awareness as well as grammar.
Initial literacy in a familiar mother tongue can support later second-language literacy, but policy and orthography vary by country.
Pedagogical grammar selects and sequences forms, and corpus evidence can show which patterns are frequent.
Pronunciation teaching targets intelligibility through phoneme contrasts, stress and intonation.
Errors reflect interlanguage and need pattern-based feedback; language awareness helps learners notice form.

en.title: Lexicography and Corpus Linguistics
en.short: How dictionaries are planned and written, and how corpora support senses, definitions and grammar.

sections.heading: Planning a dictionary
sections.text: A dictionary is planned around its users and purpose. A monolingual dictionary for advanced learners differs from a historical dictionary or a bilingual dictionary. Editors decide the word list, called the headword list, the size, the sources of evidence and the house style. They then write a style guide so that definitions, labels and examples are consistent. Good planning also sets a schedule and a checking process.

sections.heading: Entries and senses
sections.text: An entry usually gives the headword, pronunciation, part of speech, senses, definitions, examples, usage labels and cross-references. Pronunciation is often shown in the International Phonetic Alphabet, with stress and common variants; audio may be added online. Sense division groups related uses. Editors may order senses by frequency or by history, and they say which policy they follow. A definition should be clear, avoid circularity and fit the word class. A noun may be defined by a superordinate and distinguishing features.

sections.heading: Building a corpus
sections.text: A corpus is a large, structured collection of texts held in machine-readable form. Builders define the population, sample texts, record metadata such as date and region, and clear copyright. Balance and representativeness matter: a corpus should include the registers it claims to represent. Annotation may add part-of-speech tags or lemmas. A lemma is the dictionary form that groups inflected forms, such as walk for walked and walking.

sections.heading: Corpus evidence
sections.text: Software makes concordances, which show each occurrence in context, often as key word in context. Frequency counts can be raw or normalised. If a one-million-word corpus contains bank 250 times, its frequency is 250 per million, or 250 ÷ 1,000,000 = 0.025%. If 150 are financial and 100 river, the shares are 150 ÷ 250 = 60% and 100 ÷ 250 = 40%. Such evidence helps lexicographers choose headwords, order senses and write examples. It also helps grammar writing by showing which patterns are common, rare or restricted to a register.

keyPoints: A dictionary entry typically includes headword, pronunciation, part of speech, senses, definitions, examples and labels.
Sense division groups related meanings, and editors state whether they order senses by frequency or history.
A corpus is a structured, machine-readable collection built with sampling, metadata and legal care.
A concordance shows occurrences in context and supports lexicography and grammar writing.
Frequency counts should distinguish word forms from lemmas and raw from normalised figures.
Relative frequency is count ÷ corpus size, often reported per million or as a percentage.

en.title: Stylistics: Language in Literature
en.short: Foregrounding, deviation, figurative language and point of view in prose, poetry and drama.

sections.heading: Foregrounding and deviation
sections.text: Stylistics studies how language in literary texts produces meaning and effect. Its central idea is foregrounding: language made perceptible against a background. Foregrounding often comes from deviation, a departure from expected usage, and from parallelism, repeated structure. In an invented line, “The wind walked through the market”, walked is a semantic deviation because wind cannot walk; the sentence is grammatically normal. It invites a metaphorical reading. Analysis should name the norm that is broken.

sections.heading: Sound and grammar
sections.text: Phonological analysis asks about sound patterning: alliteration, assonance, rhyme, rhythm and metre. These can support tone or meaning. Grammatical analysis asks about sentence structure, word classes, clause order and repetition. A poem may use short clauses to create speed, or long complex sentences to slow reading. In prose, a shift from long to short sentences can mark tension. The analyst links each pattern to an interpretation and checks it against the whole text, not one line.

sections.heading: Figurative language and point of view
sections.text: Figurative language includes metaphor, simile, personification, metonymy (naming a thing by something associated with it, as ‘the crown’ for a king) and irony. Stylistics asks how a figure works in its context, not only what it is called. Point of view concerns the perspective from which a text speaks. It is shown by pronouns, deixis (words such as here, now, I) and modality. Pragmatic analysis asks what characters imply, presuppose or refuse to say. In drama, turn-taking and politeness can reveal power. In prose, a narrator’s words may carry a character’s viewpoint, a technique called free indirect discourse.

sections.heading: Genres and method
sections.text: Poetry invites attention to sound and line breaks. Prose invites analysis of narration, sentence rhythm and viewpoint. Drama invites analysis of dialogue, stage directions and interaction. A practical method is to choose a short passage, describe its linguistic features, explain the effect, and test the reading against the whole work. Stylistic analysis does not replace literary judgement; it gives reasons for it. It helps move from impression to evidence.

keyPoints: Stylistics explains how linguistic choices in a literary text create meaning and effect.
Foregrounding makes language perceptible through deviation from norms and through parallelism.
Phonological and grammatical analysis link sound, rhythm, syntax and word choice to interpretation.
Figurative language should be analysed in context, not merely labelled.
Point of view is signalled by pronouns, deixis and modality, and pragmatics reveals implied meaning and power.
Stylistic analysis supports prose, poetry and drama by testing interpretations against textual evidence.

en.title: Writing Systems and Orthography
en.short: Script types, the history of writing, orthographic depth and designing orthographies.

sections.heading: Types of script
sections.text:
A script is a set of written signs; a writing system pairs those signs with units of language. In a logographic script one sign stands for a word or morpheme, as in Chinese, where most characters join a meaning element to a sound element. A syllabic script has one sign per syllable, as in Linear B or the Cherokee syllabary.

Two relatives matter. An abjad writes consonants and leaves vowels to the reader, as Arabic and Hebrew largely do. An abugida adds vowel marks to a consonant sign, as Devanagari and Ethiopic do. An alphabet has separate letters for consonants and vowels, as Greek does.

sections.heading: A short history
sections.text:
In Mesopotamia, writing began with accounting. Mesopotamian clay tokens grew into cuneiform by about 3200 BCE. Egyptian hieroglyphs appear around the same time, and whether they were inspired by Mesopotamia is debated. Chinese writing is attested on oracle bones from about 1200 BCE; Maya writing was invented independently.

The Phoenician consonantal script spread across the Mediterranean, the Greeks added vowel letters, and Latin and Cyrillic descend from Greek. Hangul was created in Korea in the 1440s.

sections.heading: Orthographic depth
sections.text:
Orthographic depth is how predictable spelling is from sound. Finnish and Swahili are shallow: one letter, one sound. English is deep: the words though, through and rough share letters but not sounds, and spelling keeps traces of history and word structure, as in sign and signal.

Deep orthographies slow early reading; shallow ones are learnt faster. Depth is not a defect, because it often preserves meaning.

sections.heading: Designing orthographies
sections.text:
A practical orthography for an unwritten language is planned, not found. Steps: choose the variety to write; analyse its phonemes; pick symbols, favouring habits of the national language; mark tone if tone carries meaning; decide word division; test with speakers; check keyboard support.

Invented example: a language with /s/, /ʃ/ and three tones might write s, sh and á, a, à. Community acceptance decides success. Reform is hard: Webster changed American spellings such as color and center; Turkey adopted Latin letters in 1928.

keyPoints: A logographic sign stands for a word or morpheme; a syllabic sign for a syllable; an alphabet letter for a sound.
An abjad writes consonants only; an abugida adds vowel marks to consonant signs.
Writing arose independently in Mesopotamia, China and Mesoamerica; whether Egypt was independent is debated.
Orthographic depth is how predictable spelling is from sound; shallow systems are learnt faster.
Practical orthographies are designed with speakers, not imposed, and must suit tone and keyboards.
Spelling reform succeeds rarely and usually follows political change, as in Turkey in 1928.

en.title: Research Methods in Linguistics
en.short: Designing linguistic studies, research questions, methods, sampling, annotation, reliability and ethics.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: A study starts with a research question: a clear, answerable question about language, not a topic. Narrow it until you can say what data would count for or against your answer. Then choose a method that fits the question. A question about natural use may need a corpus or fieldwork; a question about processing may need an experiment; a question about beliefs may need a survey. State your participants, setting and analysis plan before collecting data.

sections.heading: Choosing a method
sections.text: Fieldwork records language in use, often with audio or video and detailed metadata. Elicitation asks speakers for words, sentences or judgements in controlled tasks; it is useful for rare forms but can be artificial. A corpus is a principled collection of texts or speech, often annotated, used to study frequency and patterns. Experiments control variables and measure responses such as reaction time or acceptability. Surveys use questionnaires or interviews to collect self-reports and social information.

sections.heading: Sampling and annotation
sections.text: Sampling is how you choose participants or texts. Random sampling gives every unit a known chance; stratified sampling divides the population first, for example by age or region; convenience and snowball sampling are common but biased. If 40 of 200 recorded speakers are under 25, under-25s are 40 ÷ 200 = 20% of the sample. Annotation is labelling data with a coding scheme. Write guidelines, train coders, and double-code a subset. Reliability means consistency: inter-coder agreement and test-retest checks.

sections.heading: Ethics and consent
sections.text: Ethics protects people and communities. Obtain informed consent: explain purpose, procedures, risks, benefits, data use and the right to withdraw. In community fieldwork, seek permission from relevant authorities as well as individuals, and discuss how recordings will be stored, shared and credited. Anonymise where promised. Offer practical benefit, such as copies of recordings or a community report. Follow your institution’s ethics review and local law.

keyPoints: A research question should be clear and answerable, and the method must fit it.
Fieldwork records natural use, elicitation uses controlled tasks, corpora are principled collections, and experiments and surveys answer different questions.
Sampling shapes conclusions: random and stratified samples reduce bias, and a sample share is part ÷ whole × 100, so 40 of 200 is 20%.
Annotation needs written guidelines, trained coders and double-coding.
Reliability means consistency; report inter-coder agreement and test-retest checks where relevant.
Informed consent, community permission, secure storage and fair benefit are basic ethical requirements.

en.title: Statistics and Data Analysis for Language Data
en.short: Frequency, proportion, mean, variance, correlation, hypothesis tests, chi square and regression for language data.

sections.heading: Describing data
sections.text: Frequency is a count, such as 30 tokens of a variant. Proportion is frequency divided by total: 30 ÷ 50 = 0.60, or 60%. The mean is the sum divided by n. For counts 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, the mean is 40 ÷ 5 = 8. Sample variance is Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1). The squared deviations are 16, 4, 0, 4, 16; sum 40; variance 40 ÷ 4 = 10. Correlation r measures linear association from −1 to +1 and does not prove causation.

sections.heading: Testing a claim
sections.text:
Hypothesis testing compares a pattern with chance. State a null hypothesis, choose a test and significance level, often 0.05, then compare the statistic with a critical value or report p. A p below 0.05 is often called significant, but it does not show practical importance.

Chi square tests association between categorical variables. Expected count = row total × column total ÷ grand total. Suppose dialect A has 18 variant X and 12 Y; dialect B has 7 X and 13 Y. Totals: 50, X = 25, Y = 25. Expected counts: 15, 15, 10, 10. Chi square = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E = 0.6 + 0.6 + 0.9 + 0.9 = 3.0. With df = 1, the 0.05 critical value is 3.84, so 3.0 is not significant. Report counts, χ² = 3.0, df = 1, p > 0.05. Expected counts below about 5 make it unreliable.

sections.heading: Regression and reporting
sections.text: Simple regression predicts one numerical variable from another: y = a + bx. The slope b is the predicted change in y for a one-unit rise in x; a is the intercept. R² is the share of variance in y explained by x. Report sample size, counts or summary statistics, test, statistic, df, p and effect size. For small data, exact tests or confidence intervals can be more informative than one p value.

keyPoints: Frequency is a count; proportion = frequency ÷ total.
Mean = Σx ÷ n; sample variance = Σ(x − mean)² ÷ (n − 1).
