Correlation r runs from −1 to +1 and measures linear association, not causation.
Hypothesis testing compares a statistic with a critical value or p value; p < 0.05 is often called significant but does not show importance.
Chi square = Σ(O − E)² ÷ E; expected count = row total × column total ÷ grand total; df = (rows − 1)(columns − 1).
Simple regression is y = a + bx; report n, statistic, df, p and effect size, and treat small samples with caution.

en.title: Writing the Linguistics Project
en.short: Choosing a topic, reviewing literature, collecting and analysing data, writing chapters, ethics and defence.

sections.heading: Choosing a topic
sections.text:
Choose a topic that is narrow, feasible and ethical. A broad question such as “language in Nigeria” cannot be finished well in one year. Read recent work first, then state a specific question and why it matters.

Check that you can reach speakers, texts or recordings and that your department allows the method. Agree the scope with your supervisor early.

sections.heading: Literature and sources
sections.text:
A literature review is not a list of summaries. Group sources by theme, compare their claims, and show the gap your project addresses.

Keep a record of every source, with full bibliographic details, so referencing is easier. Referencing means giving credit in the text and in a reference list, following your department’s style guide. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words or ideas as your own, including close paraphrase without citation. Check rules on self-plagiarism and collaboration.

sections.heading: Data and chapters
sections.text:
Collect data with consent and permission. Pilot your interview or recording schedule, keep field notes, and store files in named folders with backups. Analysis often means coding data into patterns and checking each claim against examples.

For instance, Amina, a final-year student in Kano, narrows a study of market greetings to fifty recorded greetings from consenting traders, then compares formal and informal terms. Write chapters in the order your department requires, often introduction, literature review, methodology, analysis and conclusion. Draft the methods and analysis early.

sections.heading: Ethics and defence
sections.text:
Data management covers consent forms, anonymisation, secure storage and retention rules. Remove names unless participants agree to be identified, and keep raw recordings separate from working copies. Follow your institution’s ethics approval process.

For the oral defence, prepare a short summary of question, method, findings and limits. Anticipate questions about sampling, bias and ethics, and practise with a colleague. Know your references and be ready to explain choices calmly.

keyPoints: Choose a narrow, feasible and ethical topic and agree its scope with your supervisor.
A literature review groups sources by theme and shows the gap your project addresses.
Referencing credits sources; plagiarism includes uncredited paraphrase.
Pilot data collection, keep backups, and anonymise personal data.
Write chapters in your department’s order and draft methods and analysis early.
Prepare for the oral defence by summarising question, method, findings and limits.

en.title: Advanced Phonological Theory: Rules, Constraints and Tone
en.short: Generative rules, Optimality Theory constraints, opacity and tone in English and African languages.

sections.heading: Frameworks compared
sections.text: Generative phonology, after Chomsky and Halle (1968), uses ordered rules to turn underlying representations into surface forms. Rule ordering explains why some forms never surface. Optimality Theory (OT), from Prince and Smolensky, uses ranked constraints: a generator makes candidates and an evaluator picks the one that best satisfies the highest-ranked constraints. Faithfulness constraints keep output close to input; markedness constraints favour unmarked structures. Related variants include Harmonic Grammar, which weights constraints instead of ranking them, and stratal OT, which applies the constraints separately at levels such as stem and word.

sections.heading: Constraints and opacity
sections.text: Constraint interaction means ranking decides conflicts: a higher-ranked constraint beats a lower one, even if the winner violates another. Opacity is when a rule applies but its effect or trigger is hidden on the surface, or when it fails to apply even though its trigger is present. Classic OT is parallel, so it handles opacity poorly; generative phonology uses rule order. OT solutions include stratal OT. In American English, /t/ often becomes a flap between vowels when the next syllable is unstressed, as in writer and latter. An OT account ranks flapping above faithfulness to /t/; a rule account states the change directly.

sections.heading: Tone representation
sections.text: Autosegmental phonology, from Goldsmith (1976), treats tone as a separate tier linked to tone-bearing units by association lines. This represents contour tones, tone spreading, floating tones and the Obligatory Contour Principle (OCP), which forbids adjacent identical tones on a tier. Yoruba, spoken in Nigeria, has high, mid and low tones; tone spreading and floating tones are analysed with these links. Akan languages of Ghana show downstep, where a high tone is lowered after another high. Such data test tone representation.

sections.heading: Evaluating analyses
sections.text: Generative phonology is explicit and handles opacity well, but rules can be numerous. OT is compact and shows universal tendencies through ranking, but classic OT struggles with opacity. Autosegmental representation is shared. When judging an analysis, ask whether it covers the data, predicts unseen forms, and uses independently needed constraints. English stress and African tone show that no single framework is universally accepted.

keyPoints: Generative phonology uses ordered rules; Optimality Theory uses ranked, violable constraints.
Constraint interaction is decided by ranking: higher-ranked constraints dominate lower-ranked ones.
Opacity is hard for classic parallel OT but natural for rule ordering; stratal OT is one response.
Autosegmental phonology represents tone on a separate tier with association lines.
Yoruba and Akan tone data test spreading, floating tones and downstep.
Judge a framework by coverage, prediction and independent motivation, not by name alone.

en.title: Advanced Syntactic Theory: Generative, Construction and Functional Approaches
en.short: Generative, construction and functional syntax; movement, binding, argument structure and Bantu evidence.

sections.heading: Three approaches
sections.text: Generative grammar, associated with Noam Chomsky, seeks a formal system that generates all and only grammatical sentences. It posits Universal Grammar and, in recent work, the Minimalist Program. Construction grammar, associated with Adele Goldberg, treats grammar as learned form-meaning pairings called constructions, with no sharp line between lexicon and syntax. Functionalist syntax, associated with Talmy Givón and Sandra Thompson, explains structures by discourse, processing and communicative needs. The approaches disagree about whether syntax is autonomous. Generative work prizes formal universals; construction grammar prizes usage and pairings; functionalism prizes function and typology.

sections.heading: Movement and binding
sections.text: Movement is displacement: a phrase is pronounced in one position but interpreted in another, leaving a trace or copy. English wh-movement forms “What did Ada buy?” from the object position. Binding theory governs pronouns and anaphors. In Chomsky’s classic formulation, an anaphor such as “herself” must be bound in its local domain; a pronoun such as “her” must be free there; a referring expression must be free. Argument structure is the set of arguments a predicate requires, with theta roles such as agent and patient. Construction grammar says constructions can add arguments, as in the caused-motion pattern. Functionalists treat transitivity as a prototype shaped by information flow.

sections.heading: Bantu evidence
sections.text: Bantu languages, spoken across much of sub-Saharan Africa, are agglutinating and rich in agreement. In Swahili, “Juma a-na-m-penda Amina” means “Juma loves Amina”: a- agrees with Juma, -na- marks present, -m- agrees with Amina, and -penda is the root. Such object marking tests argument structure: is the marker agreement or an incorporated pronoun? Verb extensions such as the applicative add an argument, producing two objects in some Bantu languages and challenging simple verb phrase structure. Wh-questions and focus constructions test movement; some Bantu languages allow in-situ wh-phrases, which functionalist and constructionist accounts handle without abstract movement. Binding domains also vary, so Bantu data refine each theory.

keyPoints: Generative grammar seeks formal rules and universal principles; construction grammar treats form-meaning pairings as basic; functionalist syntax explains structure by use.
Movement is displacement with a trace or copy; binding theory constrains anaphors, pronouns and referring expressions.
Argument structure lists a predicate’s required arguments and theta roles; constructions and discourse can also shape it.
Bantu agreement, object marking and applicatives test claims about arguments and phrase structure.
In-situ wh-phrases and variable binding domains in Bantu languages refine debates about movement and binding.
No single approach explains all data; typological evidence should decide between analyses.

en.title: Language Documentation and Endangered Languages
en.short: Recording, transcription, annotation, archiving, grammars, dictionaries, vitality and ethical community data ownership.

sections.heading: Recording and annotation
sections.text:
Language documentation makes a lasting record of a language in use; the recordings and texts are primary, not only a grammar. A common workflow is plan and consent, record, transcribe, annotate, archive. Record natural speech, interviews and stories, and label each session with date, place, speakers and rights. Use uncompressed audio such as WAV.

Transcription writes down speech. Orthographic transcription uses community spelling; phonetic transcription uses the International Phonetic Alphabet. Annotation adds translations, notes and grammatical labels, often as interlinear glossed text, where each word is glossed and each sentence is translated. Time-align segments to the audio so others can check them.

sections.heading: Archiving and outputs
sections.text:
Archiving preserves files and makes them findable. Use open, durable formats, several copies, and metadata: a catalogue record of language, place, date, speakers, rights and content. Deposit in a trusted digital archive, such as ELAR or PARADISEC, and set access levels, for example open, community-only or restricted. Persistent identifiers help others cite the collection.

Grammars and dictionaries are reference works built from the corpus. A grammar describes sounds, word structure, sentences and discourse. A dictionary lists words with meanings, examples and often audio. Speakers should check both.

sections.heading: Vitality and endangerment
sections.text: Language vitality is the strength of a language’s transmission and use. A language is endangered when children stop learning it at home and its domains, the situations where it is used, shrink. Speaker numbers alone can mislead. UNESCO’s 2003 framework assesses factors such as intergenerational transmission, domains of use, materials, official status and community attitudes. Documentation can support revitalisation, but it does not replace daily use.

sections.heading: Ethics and ownership
sections.text: Ethical fieldwork puts speakers first. Informed consent means people understand the project, risks and planned uses before agreeing. Community data sovereignty means the community decides access, reuse and deposit. Pay contributors fairly, train local researchers, and let speakers review transcripts. Protect sensitive knowledge. Invented example: Grace, a community researcher in Plateau State, Nigeria, records elders with linguist Musa; family names stay community-only and audio is restricted.

keyPoints: Language documentation creates a lasting, annotated record of a language in use, not only a grammar.
The workflow is record, transcribe, annotate, archive, then build grammars and dictionaries from the corpus.
Use open durable formats, rich metadata and a trusted archive with clear access levels.
Vitality depends on intergenerational transmission, domains of use, speaker numbers and attitudes, not numbers alone.
Informed consent and community data sovereignty mean speakers decide how recordings are used and who can access them.
Ethical fieldwork is reciprocal: fair payment, local training, community review and protection of sensitive knowledge.

en.title: Forensic Linguistics: Language, Evidence and Expertise
en.short: Authorship, legal meaning, speaker ID, police and court talk, expert limits and ethics.

sections.heading: Authorship and meaning
sections.text:
Authorship attribution infers who wrote a text from linguistic features. Analysts compare disputed texts with known samples, using idiolect (a person’s individual language habits), function words, spelling, punctuation and syntax. Stylometry applies statistics to these features. The method is probabilistic, not a fingerprint. In a hypothetical Lagos case, a court asks whether the accused wrote a threatening message. The linguist compares it with his emails and finds shared spellings but also many differences, so reports weak support.

Disputed meaning arises when a contract, statute, warning or confession is ambiguous. The linguist may describe how a word is used in a corpus, a large collection of real texts, but cannot decide the legal question. Corpus evidence informs ordinary meaning; the court interprets the law.

sections.heading: Speakers and interaction
sections.text:
Speaker identification compares a questioned recording with known voices. Forensic phoneticians examine vowels, consonants, rhythm and pitch, but voices vary with health, emotion and recording quality. A voice line-up must be fair, and the analyst should state the strength of the match. It is not a certain identification.

Police and court interaction studies how language works in legal settings. Interviewers may use leading questions, interruptions or complex cautions that suspects do not understand. Courtroom talk is asymmetric: lawyers control turns, and witnesses answer. Interpreters and vulnerable speakers need special care. These findings can improve practice and expose miscarriages of justice.

sections.heading: Limits and ethics
sections.text:
Expert linguistic evidence has limits. Samples may be short, unrepresentative or edited; comparison texts may differ in genre; and population frequencies for features are often unknown. Cognitive bias and the adversarial system can pressure experts. Admissibility rules differ by country, so check the local law.

The expert witness owes a duty to the court, not to the party paying. Ethical duties include staying within expertise, being impartial, explaining uncertainty, disclosing methods and data, and refusing to overstate. A linguist should never claim to identify a voice or author with certainty when the evidence supports only a probability.

keyPoints: Authorship attribution compares idiolect features and is probabilistic, not certain identification.
Stylometry uses statistics on function words, spelling and syntax to compare texts.
Linguists can describe disputed usage with corpus evidence, but courts decide legal meaning.
Forensic speaker comparison analyses phonetic and acoustic features and must report strength of support.
Police interviews and courtroom talk show power asymmetry; clear cautions and fair interpreting matter.
The expert’s duty is to the court: be impartial, stay within expertise and state uncertainty.
